nameStory: The "chokeberry" name comes from the intensely bitter, astringent taste of the raw berries that can literally make you pucker and feel like your throat is constricting. Despite the intimidating name, these berries are actually edible and packed with nutrients - they just need some sugar and cooking to become palatable!
description: Red chokeberry is a native New England shrub that forms spreading clumps through underground stems called suckers. It grows 6-12 feet tall with an upright, branching habit that creates dense thickets over time. In spring it produces clusters of small white or pinkish flowers, followed by bright red to dark red berries that persist well into winter.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red to dark reddish-black berries in drooping clusters, each about the size of a large pea with a small crown on the bottom. The berries feel firm and have an incredibly bitter, mouth-puckering taste if you're brave enough to try one.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink flowers in flat-topped clusters, each flower having 5 rounded petals and prominent dark pink anthers (the pollen-bearing parts). The flower clusters are about 2-3 inches across and have a subtle sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with finely toothed edges and prominent veins. They feel smooth on top but slightly fuzzy underneath, and turn brilliant orange-red to deep red in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through root suckers, creating dense thickets over time. Individual stems are smooth and grayish-brown, and the shrub maintains an upright but somewhat irregular shape.

habitat: Red chokeberry thrives in moist to wet soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade, making it common in swamps, wet meadows, and along stream banks. You'll also find it in acidic bogs and the edges of ponds throughout New England. It's adaptable enough to grow in drier sites too, including woodland borders and clearings.

seasonality.spring: Clusters of small white to pink flowers bloom in May, attracting bees and other pollinators with their sweet scent.
seasonality.summer: Green berries develop and begin turning red by late summer, while the green foliage provides dense cover.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to bright red or dark red and leaves turn spectacular shades of orange and red, making this one of our showiest fall shrubs.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red berries often remain on bare gray stems, providing food for birds and making the shrub easy to spot against snow.

funFact: Red chokeberry fruits contain some of the highest levels of antioxidants of any North American berry - even higher than blueberries and cranberries - which is why they're increasingly grown commercially and turned into health supplements and supermarket "superfruit" products.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with elderberry, but elderberry has compound leaves (leaflets arranged along a stem) while chokeberry has simple oval leaves. Also, elderberry's berries are purple-black and grow in upright clusters, while chokeberry's are red and hang downward.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name scare you away from this excellent native landscaping plant! While the raw berries are indeed bitter, they make excellent jams and jellies when cooked with sugar, and the shrub provides spectacular fall color plus winter food for wildlife.
compareHints: Red chokeberry is distinguished from its close relative black chokeberry by its red berries (black chokeberry has purple-black berries) and slightly taller growth habit. Red chokeberry also tends to prefer wetter sites, while black chokeberry is more drought-tolerant and common in drier woodlands.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black chokeberry differs from its close relative red chokeberry primarily in fruit color and leaf texture—black chokeberry has hairless leaves and black fruit, while red chokeberry has fuzzy leaf undersides and red to dark red berries.
